The provided table excerpt appears to be an **index/table-of-contents style listing** from the manual **“SIR Sectional Results – SIR Manual, Service Pack 2025-4 Build 146”** (SOFiSTiK AG). Rather than containing numerical engineering results, it organizes the document into major sections and subsections, with **page references** shown as right-aligned numbers (e.g., “1-1”, “2-1”, “3-1”, etc.). This structure is important for retrieval because it indicates where to find detailed explanations of how SIR works, what inputs it expects, and what outputs it produces.

### Table structure (as visible)
- **Column 1 (left): Section/Topic titles**
  - Examples include:
    - “Task Description”
    - “Theoretical Principles”
    - “Input Description”
    - “Output Description”
- **Column 2 (right): Page locator**
  - Examples shown include:
    - “1-1” for “Task Description”
    - “2-1” for “Theoretical Principles”
    - “3-1” for “Input Description”
    - “4-1” for “Output Description”
- **Hierarchical numbering for subsections under “Input Description”**
  - The input topics are listed with an internal numbering scheme (3.1, 3.2, …, 3.10). Each entry maps to a page range/anchor:
    - **3.1 Input Language** (page “3-1”)
    - **3.2 Input Records** (page “3-2”)
    - **3.3 CTRL – Control Parameter** (page “3-3”)
    - **3.4 SIZE – Size and Scale of the Representation** (page “3-6”)
    - **3.5 SCHH – Text Size** (page “3-8”)
    - **3.6 COLO – Selection of Colours and Line Types** (page “3-9”)
    - **3.7 GRP – Group Selection** (page “3-10”)
    - **3.8 LC – Load Case** (page “3-11”)
    - **3.9 SECT – Geometry of the Section Plane** (page “3-12”)
    - **3.10 ECHO – Output Control** (page “3-16”)

### Semantic meaning for RAG retrieval
This table functions as a **navigation map** for SIR documentation:
- Under **Input Description**, it enumerates the key **control keywords/parameters** (CTRL, SIZE, SCHH, COLO, GRP, GRP, LC, SECT, ECHO) and separates them from broader “Input Records” and “Input Language.”
- Under **Output Description**, it highlights what the user can expect to be produced, such as:
  - “List of the Forces and Moments”
  - “List of the Section Geometry”
  - “List of the Considered Load Cases”
  - “AQUA and AQB Input”
  - “Graphical Representations”

### Relationship to the provided context text
The context text describes SIR’s purpose: it defines **3D arbitrary sections** through FE structures and then computes:
- representation of intersected element types (TRUS, BEAM, CABL, QUAD, BRIC, SPRI),
- resultant **forces/moments including support reactions**,
- output data records for downstream design workflows (AQB/AQUA).

Therefore, the “Task Description” and “Input/Output Description” portions referenced in the table directly correspond to the functional summary in the surrounding excerpt. For RAG usage, this table is best indexed as a **document navigation artifact** that links parameter names (e.g., SECT, LC, ECHO) to their explanatory locations in the manual.

 Task Description
 1
 The program SIR allows the definition of three-dimensional sections through an arbitrary struc- ture. Then the following tasks are performed in this section:

3-16. 4-1. 4-1. 4-1. 4-2. 4-2. 4.5. Graphical Representations . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .. 4-2. Task Description. 1. The program SIR allows the definition of three-dimensional sections through an arbitrary struc- ture. Then the following tasks are performed in this section:.
 • Representation of the intersected elements (TRUS, BEAM, CABL, QUAD, BRIC, SPRI) and the graphical representation of their results
 • Calculation of the resultant forces and moments including the support reactions
 • Output of a data record for the dimensioning of the section with the program AQB consisting of:
 – thin-walled cross section parts (from QUAD elements)
 – thick-walled cross section parts (fom QUAD and BRIC elements)
 – tendons
 – internal forces and moments
 Thus SIR may be used for the check of FE calculations concerning the global equilibrium and for the visualisation of the results.
 On the other side SIR is an important link for the design of FE structures in the ultimate limit state. The standard FE design codes treat every element individually and do not fulfill the global compatibility of those strain states. This may lead to uneconomical or unsure results dependently on the problem.
 A consistent analysis with the limit load theory requests a considerable CPU time. If the user does not want to consider this, SIR allows to apply a classic beam design also for plane struc- tures by excising of reasonable subsystems. In this case a global ultimate limit state can be verified.
 SIR generates cross sections and internal forces and moments which can be used directly by the programs AQUA and AQB or AQBS.

First the section plane is defined. This contains a local coordinate system which corresponds to a beam coordiante system. A "‘beam"’ number and an abscissa X are used for the designation of the plane.
 First SIR determines the elements which are intersected by the defined section plane. In this case the limits at which it is possible to intersect are considered in the local coordinate system of the section.
 Then the stress state at the intersection area element - section plane is determined for the intersected elements. In this case a linear stress distribution in the element based at the results in the Gauss points is placed as a basis. The internal forces and moments of the element at the intersection area are calculated from the stress state via an integration.
 Forces of axial symmetric systems are calculated per m circumference (=QUAD thickness). SIR integrates at a circle sector. The QUAD thickness increases in radial direction. The thick- ness at cuts reference point is 1 m.
 The internal forces and moments at the intersection point beam - plane are determined with a cubic interpolation for the intersected beam and truss elements.
 SIR calculates the resultant forces and moments around the reference point after the transfor- mation of the internal forces into the local coordinate system.
 SIR is saving all forces in the database directly. Maybe the reference point is not equal to the centre of gravity of the new generated cross section. In this case additional moments are calculated due to normal force * lever arm (= distance between reference point and centre of gravity of the cross section). The reference point position should be checked therefore before further processing, e.g. a design calculation with program AQB. Perhaps the calculation has to be repeated with an adapted reference point. With the program WinGRAF it is possible to perform this iterative step interactively. Otherwise the generated input file (.SR) should be running, so that AQB may transforme all forces into the centre of gravity of cross section.
 Tendon forces lead to a stress level in the whole area element. But the tendon forces are missed during the integration of forces and moments if the cut do not hit the tendon. This could lead to unexpected results (jumps). SIR displays a warning in this case.

Otherwise the generated input file (.SR) should be running, so that AQB may transforme all forces into the centre of gravity of cross section.. Tendon forces lead to a stress level in the whole area element. But the tendon forces are missed during the integration of forces and moments if the cut do not hit the tendon. This could lead to unexpected results (jumps). SIR displays a warning in this case..
 As an further option SIR adds all support reactions in a box which is defined via a section plane and an area in front of that and behind that. All nodes and elastic bedded elements within this area, depending on the control with ECHO REAC, are used for this purpose.

The input occurs in a free format with the CADINP input language (see the general manual SOFiSTiK: ’Basics’).
 Three categories of units are distinguished:
 mm Fixed unit. Input is always required in the specified unit.
 [mm] Explicit unit. Input defaults to the specified unit. Alternatively, an explicit as- signment of a related unit is possible (eg. 2.5[m] ).
 [mm]1011 Implicit unit. Implicit units are categorised semantically and denoted by a cor- responding identity number (shown in green). Valid categories referring to the unit ”length” are, for example, geodetic elevation, section length and thickness. The default unit for each category is defined by the currently active (design code specific) unit set. This input default can be overridden as described above. The specified unit in square brackets corresponds to the default for unit set 5 (Eu- rocodes, NORM UNIT 5).

The table defines the *record structure* and the *fields/items* used within a configurable input definition for a SOFiSTiK FEA-related program section. It belongs to a larger input syntax in which the file consists of multiple blocks, each block ending with the record **END**. Inside each block, the user may adjust the **CTRL** controls and **GRP** groups “at will” (i.e., add, omit, or reorder them as allowed by the program). Additionally, the input may define multiple **SECT** sections; however, these **SECT** entries must be provided in a *pure monotonic* order with respect to the beam identification numbers and the X-values (meaning the sequence cannot jump back or repeat with respect to the ordering keys).

The table itself has two columns: **Record** and **Items**. Each row names a **record** keyword (e.g., CTRL, SIZE, SCHH, etc.) and lists the **items/fields** that record supports.

### Records and their fields
- **CTRL**: contains the control-oriented items  
  - `OPT`, `VAL`, `KIND`, `TEXT`  
  This record provides selectable options/parameters. `OPT` identifies which option is being set; `VAL` carries its value; `KIND` and `TEXT` further characterize the option or attach descriptive text.

- **SIZE**: contains size/geometry specification fields  
  - `TYPE`, `SC`, `W`, `H`, `MARG`, `FORM`, `SPLI`, `X`, `Y`, `Z`, `OPT`  
  This record defines dimensions and placement-related parameters (e.g., width/height, scaling `SC`, margins `MARG`, form/style `FORM`, split/sectioning `SPLI`, and spatial coordinates `X/Y/Z`). It also includes `OPT` for additional option control.

- **SCHH**: specifies a chain/sequence of geometric or section-related quantities  
  - `H1`, `H2`, `H3`, `H4`, `H5`, `H6`, `HE`  
  - `HL`, `HF`, `ND`  
  It appears to encode multiple height levels or thresholds (H1–H6 plus `HE`), along with lower/functional heights (`HL`, `HF`) and a count/indicator (`ND`).

- **COLO**: color-related (or attribute-related) set of items  
  - `C1`, `C2`, `C3`, `C4`, `C5`, `C6`  
  Likely assigns multiple color codes or style attributes corresponding to categories or layers.

- **GRP**: defines grouping items  
  - `NO`, `OPT`, `LAY`, `ETYP`  
  `NO` is group identifier; `OPT` selects behavior; `LAY` indicates layer; `ETYP` defines element type or group element type.

- **LC**: defines link/line/limit class or local configuration entries  
  - `NO`, `CSMI`, `CSMA`  
  `NO` identifies the entry; `CSMI`/`CSMA` define minimum/maximum capacity/section bounds or similar limits.

- **SECT**: the most complex record; defines section definitions along beams/X  
  - First line: `NO`, `XS`, `XM`, `YM`, `ZM`, `NX`, `NY`,  
    followed by: `NZ`, `NR`, `XMIN`, `XMAX`, `YMIN`, `YMAX`, `ZMIN`  
  - Next: `ZMAX`, `REF`, `SNO`, `MNO`, `SX`, `SY`, `SZ`  
  - Final: `SPEC`, `TYPm`, `TYPt`, `YSC`, `ZSC`  
  This record likely couples beam/section IDs (`NO`, `NR`, `SNO`, `MNO`) with position coordinates and extents (`XS`, `XM`, `XMIN/XMAX`, `YMIN/YMAX`, `ZMIN/ZMAX`), counts (`NX`, `NY`, `NZ`), reference behavior (`REF`), scaling for axes (`YSC`, `ZSC`), and specification/type selectors (`SPEC`, `TYPm`, `TYPt`). The critical constraint from the context is that **SECT sections must be monotonic** with respect to identifying beam numbers and X-values.

- **ECHO**: output/echo control  
  - `OPT`, `VAL`  
  Used to control what information is echoed/logged and potentially which values are reported.

### Overall semantics and ordering constraint
Because the input blocks can include **CTRL** and **GRP** entries “at will,” the essential structural requirement visible in the context is for **SECT**: multiple **SECT** definitions can be provided, but they must appear in a monotonic order aligned with beam numbering and X progression. This ensures correct interpretation when the program traverses sections along the structural member.

The following records and items are defined:
 The input consists of blocks ending with the record END. Within a block the controls CTRL or groups GRP are adjustable at will. It is also possible to define so many sections SECT as the user wants. But these sections have to be input in a pure monotonic way with respect to the identifying beam numbers and X values.
 The records HEAD, END and PAGE are described in the general manual SOFiSTiK: ’FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics’.
 It follows the description of the individual records.

The table defines the **CTRL option block for generating and exporting cross-section data for classical beam design**, specifically producing input files for **AQUA** (and optionally AQUA/QB-related workflows). It is structured as rows with columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**. Each “Item” is a named control parameter (e.g., `OPT`, `AQUA`, `SCUT`, `SPT`, `SMIN`, etc.), with an allowable numeric meaning and an associated default value.

### OPT
- **OPT** selects a literal option value from an implied list; the table shows the literal **`FULL`** as the default.
- The table also presents `OPT` used with another sub-option group (shown as `LIT`), indicating that the program can interpret different completeness/verbosity modes or output extents.

### AQUA (input file generation for program AQUA)
`AQUA` controls whether and how an **AQUA input file** is created.
- Default is shown as `*` (not fixed in the table, meaning it depends on context/other conditions).
- Key numeric modes:
  - `0`: **does not create** the AQUA file
  - `1`: create settings for **thin-walled** sections
  - `2`: **thick-walled** sections with **minimum polygon points**
  - `3`: thick-walled sections with **condensed element edges**
  - `4`: thick-walled sections as **single polygons**
  - `6`: like mode `2`, but create **SREC cross sections if possible**
  - `14`: like mode `6`, but **ignore different material numbers** in section parts
- The table implies these modes affect the **geometric discretization/representation** of cross-sections used in downstream beam design.

### SCUT (control of shear cuts in AQUA)
- **SCUT**: controls whether **shear cuts** are generated.
- Unit is `–`.
- Default is `-1`.
- Meaning:
  - `<0`: **without control**, uses the **AQUA default**
  - `0`: **without shear cuts**
  - `>0`: **use AQUA manual** behavior

### SPT (additional stress points in AQUA output)
- **SPT** controls whether additional stress points are created.
- Unit is `–`.
- Default is `*` (context-dependent).
- Meaning:
  - `0`: do **not** create
  - `1`: **create** stress points

### SMIN (default of first cross-section numbers / deletion behavior)
- **SMIN** governs the default numbering strategy for cross-sections.
- Unit is `–`.
- Default is `0`.
- Meaning:
  - `<0`: **not used** for SIR cross-sections; additionally, SIR cross-sections are **deleted from the database** if `CTRL AQUA > 0`
  - `>0`: without deleting
  - `0`: find a **minimum** cross-section number
  - `-10000`: like `0`, but with **deleting**

### AQBS
The bottom portion begins a row for:
- **AQBS**: “Input file for AQBS”
- Default is not visible in the provided crop, but the pattern indicates it mirrors the logic of AQUA (i.e., controls whether an input file is created and potentially which variant is generated).

Overall, the table is a **parameter specification** for configuring how cross-section geometry (thin/thick, polygon complexity, shear cut inclusion, stress point generation) and how cross-section numbering/management (SMIN) are handled when exporting results to **AQUA/AQBS** workflows.

The table describes **CTRL options** that control how the program **SIR** (generating cross-section data and internal forces) writes/exports results for **AQUA** and **AQB** (used later for classical beam design). It is presented as a key–value style list with *Item*, *Description*, *Unit*, and *Default* values, followed by detailed behavior notes. Many options regulate geometric tolerance during cutting, integration/extrapolation rules for volume/QUAD elements, reinforcement handling for QUAD regions, and where stresses are reported.

Key entries:

- **V2MT – file with internal forces (and combination logic)**  
  Unitless integer. Default described as **2**. Controls how plate shear/torques are combined into torsional moments:
  - `-1` / `0` / `1` / `2`-style behaviors are specified:
    - `0`: does **not** add plate shear into torsional moments; additionally, the **m-xy** part of **QUAD** elements is added **twice**.
    - `1`: **adds once** (m-xy from QUAD elements added once).
    - `2` (default): **adds** plate shear parts from the plate shear **into** torsional moments with the specified rule.
  Purpose: define how internal force components are mapped when exporting to files for beam design.

- **TOLG – Geometric tolerance for cutting**  
  Default shown as **-1.0**. It provides a tolerance factor controlling the “cut” operation. Sign indicates whether the default is used or modified:
  - `m < 0`: use default,
  - `m > 0`: scale/override default by factor `m`.

- **TOLP – Geometric tolerance for generating the m/− polygon**  
  Default also **-1.0** with similar sign semantics:
  - negative means use default,
  - positive means apply the factor to control **maximum polygon edge length** (noted indirectly later).
  This tolerance strongly affects whether polygon edges become too short (leading to disappearance of edges and unusable cross sections).

- **LCR – design case number of QUAD reinforcements**  
  Default `-1` with meaning:  
  - `-1`: don’t use QUAD reinforcements,
  - other values: enable reinforcement use based on design case selection.

- **BRIC – control of integration of volume elements**  
  Default `0`. Defines extrapolation/integration strategy:
  - `0`: extrapolate node values from Gauss points,
  - `1`: use value at the **element middle** for the whole element.

- **TEND – control of integration of QUAD tendons**  
  Default `0`.  
  - `0`: no integration of tendons,
  - `1`: perform integration of tendons.

- **VAL – Value of the option**  
  Generic field with description indicating the option’s numeric value (used by CTRL).

- **SPT points (LT / Z-Point / Y±Point)**  
  A point-selection scheme for where stresses are evaluated:
  - **LT** / Z- and Z+ / Y- and Y+ “Point at min.Z / middle Z / max.Z, middle”
  - and similarly for **Y**: **Point at max.Y, middle** and **Point at min.Y, middle**.  
  The text notes that Z- and Z+ are used as default for thick-walled cross sections.

- **Context-specific behavior and defaults for CTRL AQUA / CTRL AQB**  
  The table is accompanied by narrative specifying defaults chosen when **CTRL AQUA** is not provided, depending on database content:
  - If **BRIC elements were found** → default `CTRL AQUA 2`.
  - If the **first cut beam cross section is thick-walled** → default `CTRL AQUA 2`.
  - Otherwise:
    - sections with **beams/trusses/cables** default to `CTRL AQUA 1`,
    - sections intersecting only **QUAD elements** default to `CTRL AQUA 2`.
  For **curved structures**, QUAD elements may intersect each other; since this cannot be represented for solid elements in AQUA, it recommends **CTRL AQUA 1** in such cases.

Overall, the table functions as a specification of how to:
1) **Export internal forces** (V2MT mapping rules),  
2) **Perform robust geometric cutting/polygon generation** (TOLG, TOLP),  
3) **Choose reinforcement usage and integration strategies** (LCR, BRIC, TEND), and  
4) **Select stress evaluation points** (SPT LT variants),  
with additional guidance on how AQUA defaults depend on the detected element types in the database and structural geometry.

 The results of SIR can be stored in an input file for the programs AQUA and AQB for the use
 of a classical beam design. The kind and the extent of these dates are described with the corresponding CTRL options.
 If nothing is input for CTRL AQUA, CTRL AQUA 2 is used as default if BRIC elements were found in database. The same default is set if the first cut beam cross section is thick-walled. Otherwise CTRL AQUA 1 is used as default for sections with beams, trusses or cables. The default of sections which intersect only QUAD elements is CTRL AQUA 2. In the case of curved structures the QUAD elements can be intersected each other. Because such intersection is unrepresentable for solid elements in AQUA, it is recommended to use CTRL AQUA 1.

Otherwise CTRL AQUA 1 is used as default for sections with beams, trusses or cables. The default of sections which intersect only QUAD elements is CTRL AQUA 2. In the case of curved structures the QUAD elements can be intersected each other. Because such intersection is unrepresentable for solid elements in AQUA, it is recommended to use CTRL AQUA 1..
 The stress points ’Z-’ and ’Z+’ are generated as default of CTRL SPT for thickwalled cross sections.
 For SIR, it is relatively difficult to find a suitable default of CTRL TOLG / TOLP for any system. Unfortunately, the oriention to the system dimensions is not possible, because even in a large system there can be areas with very small elements that are to be cut. This leads to very short polygonal edges. A too large CTRL TOLP (= maximum length of polygon edges in the gener- ated cross-section) causes these edges to disappear completely, which can lead to unusable cross-sections. Therefore it is sometimes more useful to set the geometrical tolerance of the cuts with CTRL TOLG more wide / finer. Then the decision for one of the two found QUAD elements is more clearly when cutting nearby QUAD edges.
 Instead of an input with SECT in the program AQUA for every section the cross section num- bers can be defined also in a pure monotonic way with respect to this number via CTRL SMIN.
 SIR calculates the sum of a QUAD reinforcement determined by BEMESS with CTRL LCR > 0 and ECHO REIN YES/FULL.

The table defines configuration parameters for generating paper output (plots/sheets) and controlling how drawings are laid out, scaled, bordered, partitioned, oriented, and rendered. It is structured as rows of individual “items,” each with a short purpose (“Description”), a unit, and a default value.

**TYPE** (default: -4, unit: “–”): Specifies the paper size/type and implicitly controls orientation by sign. A **positive value** selects a **landscape** format, while a **negative value** selects **portrait**. The values correspond to standard paper or printer/publisher formats, including DIN-like sizes (A, B, C, D), American ANSI sizes (A–D), and Hewlett-Packard plotter formats (e.g., HPA–HPD, HP1–HP4, with explicit dimensions given in the surrounding context). The additional text notes that TYPE can also select special formats (e.g., for Hewlett-Packard plotters) and that a preceding minus sign switches portrait orientation.

**SC** (default: `*`, unit: “–”): Controls the drawing scale. A value of **0** means “format filling” (largest possible drawing regardless of scale). An asterisk (`*`) indicates the software chooses an **engineering scale** to best fill the page, using common ratios like **1:1, 1:2, 1:5** and their multiples. (A separate rule in the context also states that if an explicit SC is set and technically feasible, that setting is used.)

**W** and **H** (paper width and height, units: `cm`, defaults: `TYPE`): Define the paper dimensions directly. If W and/or H are set to **0**, the program automatically selects an appropriate paper size; if only one dimension is zero, the other direction is fitted and the scale does not need explicit definition.

**MARG** (default: `FULL`, unit: `LIT`): Determines the border and effective margins. Options:
- **NO** (default behavior for single-sheet printers, per text): draws an inner border and uses **W and H** to define the drawing area.
- **YES**: draws a free border around the drawing, with **W/H defining paper size**; otherwise a margin rule applies (noted: ~2 cm margin, otherwise ~0.5 cm).
- **FULL**: adds an additional border so the drawing is cut to outer paper limits (noted as relevant for drum plotters).

**FORM** (default: `*`, unit: `LIT`): Chooses the border frame style: **STAN** (standard frame), **ZTVK** (ZTVK-88 frame), or **URS** (Report Browser definition). Default is shown as `*`, meaning a system-defined choice unless overridden.

**SPLI** (default: `1x1`, unit: `LIT`): Controls how the output paper is partitioned into multiple sheets/tiles.
- Default **1x1** means no partitioning (single sheet).
- Other partitioning modes (from surrounding context) include **HxW (height × width)**, indicating how the large output is split across sections.

**X, Y, Z** (units: `degree`, defaults: X=330, Y=180, Z=270): Define the angles of the coordinate axes relative to the horizontal, effectively controlling the projection/orientation of the rendered view. This is crucial for consistent visualization across plots.

**OPT** (default: `1`, unit: `–`): Sets an option controlling the graphical representation style/behavior. The surrounding context implies these options affect how drawings are produced (with default representation mode = 1).

**Relationship to the additional context:**  
The accompanying text clarifies operational behavior (how paper format is selected via TYPE or W/H, how SC=0 forces maximum filling, and that SIZE SPLI causes creation of new sheets for different partitions—potentially also generating additional sheets per load case or component for certain OPT modes). It also mentions that the user can select the paper format implicitly (TYPE) or explicitly (W/H), and it provides a larger rule set for scaling and pagination.

 • The user selects the paper format either implicitly using TYPE or explicitly by the width W and the height H. The program can set the scale itself by picking the largest possible scale with the common values of 1:1, 1:2 and 1:5 or their multiples. An explicit setting of the scale SC will be used, if technically feasible. Setting SC to 0 results in the largest possible drawing regardless of the scale.
 • The user specifies the scale and by setting W and/or H to zero the appropriate paper size is automatically chosen. If only one of the two values is set to zero, then the drawing size will be automatically calculated to fit in the second direction, the scale does not need to be defined in this case.

This table defines a set of configurable sizing and formatting parameters for a given record, identified by “Item” codes H1–H6 and HE–HF, plus ND. The structure is a parameter registry with four columns: **Item** (parameter code), **Description** (human-readable meaning), **Unit** (measurement unit), and **Default** (default value used by the system).

### Header/General context
- The table content appears to relate to **SCHH** (as referenced in the surrounding context), which likely governs **text sizing and representation scaling** per input record **SIZE**.
- Additional context states: **text sizes are re-initialized for every input of the record SIZE**. If a text size is set to **zero**, “no designation occurs” (i.e., that element is not assigned/rendered).
- It also notes: **values HE to HF are preset in a smaller way for multiple representations (SIZE SPLI)**, implying that the maximum allowable sizes depend on whether multiple representations are active.

### Parameter definitions (Item codes)

**H1–H6 (all in cm)**
1. **H1 – Legend (Unit: cm; Default: \*)**  
   Represents the **legend text size**. The default is an asterisk, meaning it is likely **paper-size dependent** rather than a fixed numeric value.
2. **H2 – Element numbers (Unit: cm; Default: H1)**  
   Controls the size of **element number labels**. Default behavior ties it directly to **H1**, indicating consistent scaling between legend and element numbering.
3. **H3 – Stresses (Unit: cm; Default: H2·0.7)**  
   Determines the size used for **stress values**. Default is derived from **H2** using a multiplier of **0.7**, producing smaller text than element numbers.
4. **H4 – not used (Unit: cm; Default: —)**  
   Placeholder indicating this parameter is inactive.
5. **H5 – Scales (Unit: cm; Default: H3)**  
   Sets the size of **scale labels**; default is aligned with **H3** to maintain proportionality.
6. **H6 – not used (Unit: cm; Default: —)**  
   Another inactive placeholder.

### Maximum size constraints (HE–HF, all in cm)
7. **HE – Maximum size for single forces (Unit: cm; Default: 4.0)**  
   Upper bound for how large single-force annotations may be.
8. **HL – Maximum size for line forces (Unit: cm; Default: 3.0)**  
   Upper bound for line-force annotations.
9. **HF – Maximum size for area forces (Unit: cm; Default: 2.0)**  
   Upper bound for area-force annotations.  
Contextually, these maxima may be **reduced** under **multiple representations** via **SIZE SPLI**, to keep overall graphics readable.

### Decimal formatting (ND)
10. **ND – Number of decimal places after comma (Unit: —; Default: -)**  
   Controls numeric formatting precision. The description further indicates it can be derived from:
   - “default from” (implied system setting), and
   - **SOFISTIK units** (suggesting unit-aware default precision).

Overall, the table establishes a **hierarchical default scheme** for text sizing (H1→H2→H3→H5) and applies **cap limits** for force annotation sizes (HE/HL/HF), while also specifying **numeric display precision** (ND).

See also: SIZE, COLO
 SCHH
 The text sizes are re-initialized for every input of the record SIZE. If a text size is defined with zero, no designation occurs.
 The values HE to HF are preset in a little bit smaller way for multiple representations (SIZE SPLI).

The table lists configurable line-type settings for a legend and for stress/field visualization components in a SOFiSTiK-related plotting or graphics context. It is organized into four columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**. All entries use a unit of “–”, indicating that these parameters are categorical style identifiers (not physical quantities).

### Items and meanings
- **C1 – Line type of the legend**  
  Defines how the legend’s line is drawn (i.e., the style representing the plotted quantity in the legend).  
  **Default:** `1001`.

- **C2 – Line type of the intersection lines**  
  Specifies the line style used for intersection lines in the visualization (e.g., where surfaces or regions intersect in the graphical output).  
  **Default:** `1001`.

- **C3 – Line type of the positive stresses**  
  Sets the line style for positive stress results (often tension/positive sign depending on convention).  
  **Default:** `4001`.

- **C4 – Line type of the negative stresses**  
  Sets the line style for negative stress results (often compression/negative sign).  
  **Default:** `2001`.

- **C5 – reserved for further line type**  
  Placeholder entry for additional future or optional line-type settings not specified in this excerpt.  
  **Default:** (blank/not provided).

- **C6 – reserved for further line type**  
  Another placeholder for future expansion of line-type definitions.  
  **Default:** (blank/not provided).

### How the numeric codes are interpreted (context)
The surrounding context explains that a **four-digit number** `nnnn` defines the visual line pattern. The **last digit** controls the dot/dash pattern style, for example:
- `1` = solid  
- `2` = dashed  
- `3` = dotted  
- `4` = dots and dashes  
- `5` = tight dashes  
- `6` = tight dots  
- `7` = tight dots and dashes  
- `8` = spaced dashes  
- `9` = spaced dots  

The **first digit** indicates the **pen number**, i.e., the drawing color/style index. Example: `3003` means a dotted line using pen `3` (green), and default color mapping is given as:
- `1` black/white, `2` red, `3` green, `4` blue, `5` yellow, `6` magenta, `7` cyan, `8` brown.

This directly relates to the table defaults: e.g., `4001` and `2001` imply different pen/color choices for positive vs. negative stress lines, while ending with `1` indicates **solid** pattern for all specified defaults shown (`C1–C4`).

The input table defines parameters for selecting and controlling how element data is processed within an analysis workflow (notably for integration of internal stresses and moments). Each row represents an input “Item” with a corresponding “Description,” an “Unit,” and a “Default” value. The “See also” references (“CTRL, SECT, GRP”) indicate that this table is part of a larger set of controls where GRP-style grouping and selection logic affects subsequent computations.

### Columns
- **Item**: The parameter name used as an input field.
- **Description**: What the parameter controls and allowable values.
- **Unit**: Unit of the parameter (shown as **–** for non-physical identifiers or option fields).
- **Default**: Program default behavior when the parameter is not explicitly provided.

### Parameters
1. **NO (Group number)**
   - **Meaning**: Selects a *group* of elements for the operation being configured.
   - **Unit**: **–** (identifier only).
   - **Default**: `*` (meaning: use all group numbers by default).
   - **Context link**: The accompanying text states that *only elements with the selected group numbers are considered for the integration of internal stresses and moments*. If no selection is made, the default is to use **all** group numbers. It further notes: “The default NO is set for all groups with the input of the first record GRP.”

2. **OPT (Option)**
   - **Meaning**: Controls whether something is used, and optionally whether members are printed.
   - **Unit**: **LIT** (indicating it is a literal/keyword enumeration).
   - **Default**: `FULL`.
   - **Allowed values**:
     - `OFF`: “do not use”
     - `YES`: “use”
     - `FULL`: “use and print the members”
   - **Interpretation**: This parameter is best understood as a switch controlling both activation and output verbosity.

3. **LAY (Layer of the reinforcement)**
   - **Meaning**: Specifies the reinforcement layer for cross-section descriptions.
   - **Unit**: **–**.
   - **Default**: `-` (not set).
   - **Context link**: If **LAY is defined**, then **TRUSS** and **QUAD** reinforcements are used *with this layer* when describing the cross section.

4. **ETYP (Element type)**
   - **Meaning**: Filters or classifies which element types are relevant to the operation.
   - **Unit**: **LIT** (keyword list).
   - **Default**: `-` (no restriction specified).
   - **Allowed values**:
     - `-` All element types
     - `BEAM` Beam elements
     - `TRUS` Truss elements
     - `CABL` Cable elements
     - `QUAD` QUAD elements and their tendons
     - `BRIC` Volume (brick) elements
     - `SPRI` Coupling spring elements
   - **Interpretation**: ETYP acts as a categorical selector. In combination with **LAY**, it becomes especially important for identifying the reinforcement-containing element families (notably **TRUS** and **QUAD**).

### Grouping logic (from the additional context)
The table’s **NO (group number)** ties to an internal rule: *the group number of an element equals the element number divided by the group divisor* (referenced as program **SOFiMSHA**). This means selection is not arbitrary; it is derived from element numbering and a configured divisor, aligning group selection with how the model is partitioned for stress/moment integration.

See also: CTRL, SECT
 GRP
 Only the elements with the selected group numbers are considered for the integration of the internal stresses and moments. The default is the use of all group numbers. The default NO is set for all groups with the input of the first record GRP.
 If LAY is defined, the TRUSS and QUAD reinforcements are used as reinforcement with this layer for the cross section descriptions.
 The group number of an element is equal to the element number divided by the group divisor (see program SOFiMSHA).

The input table defines options related to prestress treatment in terms of load case numbers and the inclusion of statically determinate prestress components. It contains three columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**. The table is intended for users configuring load-case-based evaluation in prestressed concrete analysis workflows (cross-referenced by the provided context mentioning **LC**, **CSMI**, **CSMA**, and subsequent creep/shrinkage processing).

### Row 1
- **Item: NO**
- **Description: Load case number**
- **Unit: —**
- **Default: !** (required/mandatory)

This row specifies the identifier for the load case being defined or modified. The “!” in the Default column indicates that a valid load case number must be provided by the user. In the surrounding context, the term **LC** is used to denote a load case, and the integration of stresses and moments occurs “in every following defined section for every selected load case.” Therefore, this field controls which particular LC is affected by the prestress/construction-stage settings.

### Row 2
- **Item: CSMI**
- **Description: Addition of the statically determinate parts of the pre-stress for the tendons with the construction stages CSMI and CSMA**
- **Unit: —**
- **Default: -**

This field controls whether and how statically determinate components of prestress are added for tendons associated with construction stages labeled **CSMI** and **CSMA**. From the contextual text:
- The analysis distinguishes between statically determinate and statically indeterminate parts of prestress.
- If this option is **used**, the statically determinate parts computed from selected tendons using **CSMI** and **CSMA** are added to the resultant internal forces and moments.
- If this option is **not** used, then prestress is treated as the inherent stress state, meaning only the statically indeterminate parts remain in resultant internal forces and moments.
Thus, **CSMI** acts as a configuration switch/selector for the addition of determinately computed prestress contributions tied to those construction stages.

### Row 3
- **Item: CSMA**
- **Description not explicitly shown in the snippet**
- **Unit: —**
- **Default: CSMI**

In the excerpt, the row header **CSMA** is present, with its default set to **CSMI**. This implies a coupled configuration: **CSMA** likely mirrors or inherits the value/setting of **CSMI** unless explicitly changed. In practical terms, it means construction-stage handling for tendons is governed by both labels, and the default behavior assumes **CSMA = CSMI**.

### Overall table meaning
Collectively, the table configures **(1)** which **load case number (NO/LC)** is targeted and **(2)** whether prestress contributions from **statically determinate parts** are incorporated based on construction-stage definitions **CSMI** and **CSMA**. This is particularly relevant because, as noted in the context, creep and shrinkage handling for difference load cases (created via “CTRL DIFF …”) depends on how prestressing steel effects are included or excluded in subsequent program steps (e.g., results stored to isolate the concrete part, and **SIR** avoiding recalculation of prestressing-steel contributions).

See also: SECT
 LC
 The integration of the stresses and moments is performed in every following defined section for every selected load case.
 The statically determinate parts of the prestress are determined from the selected tendons with CSMI and CSMA. These parts are added to the resultant internal forces and moments. Without this option the prestress is the inherent stress state. It means that only the statically indeterminate parts of the prestress remain in the resultant internal forces and moments.
 Creep+shrinkage for QUAD tendons:
 In program ASE it is possible to calculate difference load cases from the sum load cases (CTRL DIFF ...).
 The losts due to creep and shrinkage (without prestressing steel) of these difference load cases are necessary for the design with program AQB. They should be calculated therefore with the program SIR in order to prevent a new creep calculation in AQB.
 In the program ASE the results of these difference load cases are saved in a special way in order to consider only the concrete part. Thus SIR ignores the part of the prestressing steel.
 The SIR results of the difference load cases are therefore not equal to the simple difference of the initial (sum) load cases (because the part of the prestressing steel is not available).
 You can find an example for that with more hints in program TEDDY at csm4_quad_singlespan.dat
 Example:
 In program ASE the construction stage creep and shrinkage 15 (CS 15) is stored in load case 4015 (LC 4015) (=sum load case for creep and shrinkage).
 Then in ASE the difference load case 5015 (=difference load case creep and shrinkage) is created by using the control LC DIFF 1000 (an automatic procedure in program CSM).
 Now in SIR only the difference load cases (LC 5015) should be used for calculation. Note that the construction stages input (LC CSMI) has to be used for load cases with prestress.

The table defines the **input record format for one SECT entry**, i.e., the description of a **beam cross-section cut** used during internal force evaluation in SIR. SECT records are processed for all **load cases** and **groups**; geometry and internal forces are evaluated for every defined section within an input block. A section is identified by a **beam section number (NO)** and an **ordinate (XS)** along the beam; sections with the same NO belong to the same “beam” and can be visualized together (e.g., in WinGraf). The first SECT input typically **clears previously stored sections and their results** from the database.

### Main identification and position (beam axis)
- **NO (Section number)**: Integer identifier of the section group along the beam. Default **1**.
- **XS (Beam ordinate)**: Position along the beam in meters. Default **0.0 m**.  
  If XS is not given, the program calculates it from the distance to the last reference point (XM, YM, ZM).

### Reference point and section plane normal
- **XM, YM, ZM (Global coordinates of the reference point)**: The origin of the section plane (cross-section plane) in global coordinates, in meters. Defaults **0**.
- **NX, NY, NZ (Components of the section normal)**: Direction of the section plane normal vector; unitless components with defaults **0**.

### Local coordinate system orientation
Two alternative ways determine orientation of the section’s **local y-axis** (with the section normal defining the local x-axis direction):
- **NR (Reference axis / orientation selector)**: A literal (listed as **XX, YY, ZZ, NEGX, NEGY, NEGZ**) indicating the global axis used to construct the local y-axis plane relative to the area normal. Unit: **LIT**. Default unspecified (shown as `*`), meaning it is optional and if omitted different default orientation rules apply.
- **SX, SY, SZ (Components of the local y-axis vector)**: Explicit vector defining the plane direction for the local y-axis. Default **0,0,0**.  
  Exactly how NR vs. SX/SY/SZ is used matches the described options: if neither is provided, the local z-axis aligns with gravity and the section y-axis becomes parallel to the global XY plane (subject to normal-vs-gravity alignment); otherwise the local y direction lies in the plane defined by the area normal and the chosen axis/vector.

Additionally:
- **REF (Reference type or node)**: How the reference point (XM/YM/ZM) may be defined relatively, e.g., relative to a structural node or relative to a QUAD element centre (when REF QUAD is used). Unit **LIT**.

### Support and clipping window geometry
The section plane is clipped using:
- **XMIN, XMAX (Active range for support reactions)**: Limits in meters; defaults **-0.001** and **+0.001**.
- **YMIN, YMAX, ZMIN, ZMAX (Local clipping window)**: Bounds in meters, defined in the section plane’s local coordinate system relative to the reference point. Defaults are wide open: **YMIN=-99, YMAX=+99, ZMIN=-99, ZMAX=+99**.

These parameters define which parts of intersected geometry are included in the section cut evaluation and which support influence region is active.

### Section-to-material / cross-section identification
- **SNO (Cross section number)**: The cross-section definition index used for material/section properties; default `*` (required/depends on context).
- **MNO (Material number of this section + 1000·material number of reinforcement)**: Encodes the material selection; default `*`.

### Additional options
- **SPEC (Special options of section)**: Modifier flags for special behaviors (unit `Lit4`), default `-`.

An example shown in the context is **A = related to start of beam**.

Overall, this SECT table specifies: (1) where the cut occurs along the beam (NO, XS, and computed spacing logic), (2) how the cut plane is positioned and oriented (XM/YM/ZM, NX/NY/NZ, NR or SX/SY/SZ), (3) what geometric region is considered (local clipping window and active support range), and (4) which cross-section/material definition is applied (SNO/MNO) along with optional special behaviors (SPEC).

sections: 3.9 SECT – Geometry of the Section Plane

content:
The input table fragment describes the **SECT** section-definition block used by the program to evaluate geometry and internal forces along a beam. It specifies that, within each **input block**, an evaluation is performed **for all defined load cases and groups** for **all sections** included in the block.

A key aspect is the **database management and result reset** behavior: the **first** SECT entry instructs the system to **delete all previously stored sections** and also **delete all stored section results**. Therefore, SECT entries act as a complete redefinition of the section set for subsequent calculations.

Sections are organized as **beam sections**: each section belongs to one “beam” if it has the same **beam number**, enabling consistent graphical display in **WinGraf**. Each section is identified by a **beam section number** and an **ordinate XS**. If XS is **not provided**, it is **calculated** from the difference to the previous reference point **(XM, YM, ZM)**. A default behavior is stated: SIR maintains the **last defined NO**, and the **very first NO defaults to 1**.

The table defines the **cross-section plane geometry** using multiple components:
1. **Reference point** of the plane (origin of the cross section).
2. A **local coordinate system** derived from the **section normal vector**:
   - the **section normal** defines the local **x-axis direction** (orientation of the plane normal),
   - the local **y-axis** orientation is defined separately (see below).
3. A **clipping window** in the local coordinates: **YMIN, YMAX, ZMIN, ZMAX** to limit the area considered.
4. An **active range for supports**: **XMIN, XMAX** controlling which portion of the beam participates for support-related evaluation.

Orientation of the **local y-axis** is controlled in one of three ways:
- If **NR is not input** and **SX, SY, SZ are not input**, the local **z-axis** aligns with **gravity**. If the cut normal is parallel to gravity (noted for “column” cases), then the local y-axis becomes parallel to the **global XY plane**.
- If **NR** is given with literal direction keywords (e.g., **XX, YY, ZZ, NEGX, NEGY, NEGZ**), the local y-axis lies in a plane defined through the **area normal** and the selected **global coordinate axis**. Again, if the cut normal is parallel to gravity, the local y-axis is parallel to the global XY plane.
- If **SX, SY, SZ** are input (vector definition), the local y-axis lies in the plane defined through the **area normal** and the provided vector.

For defining the reference point relative to structure, the table explains optional use of a **reference definition**:
- Using a **reference node** at **REF**, the reference point may be defined **relatively** to a structural node.
- If **REF QUAD** is used, the reference point is defined relative to the **center of the QUAD element** (**NREF**), otherwise the default orientation comes from the element itself.

Additional geometric/FE interaction rules are included:
- If no reference material is provided for AQUA cross-section definition, the **first intersected element** is used.
- If a section plane lies exactly along a **QUAD edge**, the plane can intersect **two QUAD elements**; only the element located **behind the plane** (in the direction of the section-plane normal) is used.
- The **warping moment Mb from QUAD elements** is calculated **only if** shear-center coordinates **YSC and ZSC** are provided.

Finally, the table notes fallback behavior:
- If **no SECT record** exists, sections already stored in the database are reused, which can be managed via **WinGraf**.
- All defined sections are saved to the database and can be verified or modified in WinGraf.

sections: 3.9 SECT – Geometry of the Section Plane

content:
The table defines a set of input items used to parameterize **cross-sectional definitions** for structural analysis, including how sections are treated for bending behavior and how related reference data (e.g., shear centre and coordinate reference) are provided.

## Columns
- **Item**: Identifier of the parameter (e.g., TYPY, YSC).
- **Description**: Meaning of the parameter and—where relevant—enumerated allowed values.
- **Unit**: Physical unit expected by the input (empty where not applicable or dimensionless).
- **Default**: The system default value if the user does not specify the parameter.

## Items and meaning

### 1) `B` and `C` (member enforcement flags)
These are listed as possible values under a higher-level grouping (context: enforcement behavior):
- `B`: *enforce bending member*
- `C`: *enforce compression member*
No units or defaults are shown for these flags, implying they are qualitative mode selections rather than numeric parameters.

### 2) `TYPm` (Type of section for **main bending**)  
- **Item**: `TYP M` (displayed as `TYP M` in the table)
- **Description**: Chooses the section category used to evaluate **main bending**.
- **Default**: `SECT`
- **Unit**: not applicable (shown blank)
- **Allowed/defined section types** (enumerated in the description):
  - `SECT` — Regular section
  - `FACE` — Face of a clamped support
  - `HFAC` — Face of a support with articul. connection (masonry)
  - `IFAC` — Section at the face of an indirect support
  - `SHEA` — Critical section for shear design
The default `SECT` indicates that, unless overridden, the regular section is used for main bending evaluation.

### 3) `TYPT` (Type of section for **transverse bending**)  
- **Item**: `TYP T`
- **Description**: Chooses the section category used for **transverse bending**.
- **Default**: `SECT`
- **Unit**: not applicable
- **Allowed types**: same set as for main bending:
  `SECT`, `FACE`, `HFAC`, `IFAC`, `SHEA`.

### 4) `YSC` and `ZSC` (Coordinates of the shear centre)
These parameters support warping-related calculations and shear centre reference.
- **`YSC`**: shear centre coordinate in the **Y-direction**
  - **Unit**: `m`
  - **Default**: `-` (meaning no default / not set by default)
- **`ZSC`**: shear centre coordinate in the **Z-direction**
  - **Unit**: `m`
  - **Default**: `-`  
**Functional implication (from the provided context):** the warping moment from QUAD elements (`Mb`) is calculated only if **both** shear centre coordinates are input (i.e., YSC and ZSC must be provided).

### 5) `NREF` (Reference element for REF)
- **Item**: `NREF`
- **Description**: “Reference element to REF”
- **Unit**: dimensionless (shown as `–`)
- **Default**: `–` (no default)
**Functional implication (from context):** `NREF` is used when the section’s reference point (REF) is defined relative to a structural element rather than absolute coordinates. The section reference point can be tied to element geometry (e.g., the centre of a QUAD element), ensuring consistent placement of the section plane.

## Overall role in section evaluation
Together, these items control **which section definition** is used for different bending checks (main vs transverse) and provide **geometric/reference data** required for correct positioning and advanced mechanics (shear centre/warping). This aligns with the broader SECT mechanism described in the context: sections are defined and evaluated per load cases/groups, with optional use of stored section definitions when no new SECT record is provided.

The provided table is an **options/configuration summary** for an SIR post-processing output routine (cross-section evaluation). It is structured with the columns **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**. The **Item** column contains two main categories: **OPT** (output options) and **VAL** (value selection for an output option).

---

## Rows under **Item = OPT**
These rows define what additional information SIR will generate for the considered section and load cases. The **Unit** column is effectively not used for meaningful physical units; it mostly contains **“LIT”** (indicating a literal/keyword choice). The **Default** column provides the default behavior for each keyword.

### 1) **OPT**
A group selector meaning: *“A literal from the following list:”*  
- **Default:** `-` (no direct default for the group; each sub-option has its own default)

### 2) Geometry/section definition outputs
- **GEO**: *Geometry of the section*  
  - **Unit:** `LIT`  
  - **Default:** **YES**  
  - Meaning: outputs geometric data describing the section and intersected elements.

### 3) Support reaction outputs
- **REAC**: *Support reactions in the section*  
  - **Unit:** `LIT`  
  - **Default:** **NO**  
  - Meaning: enables printing of nodal forces/moments aggregated for the section per load case.

Additional context from the surrounding text (relevant to this table) clarifies how **support reactions** are handled when enabled:
- With `ECHO REAC YES/FULL/EXTR/4`, reactions are printed per load case.
- **All nodes inside the section box** are used, independent of group control.
- `EXTR` adds forces from **bedding of area elements** (using area-element-based contribution).
- `4` uses the bedding resulting forces instead of node support forces.

### 4) Reinforcement outputs
- **REIN**: *QUAD reinforcement(s)*  
  - **Unit:** `LIT`  
  - **Default:** **YES**  
  - Meaning: outputs reinforcement-related components for the section.

### 5) Internal force outputs (forces/moments)
- **FORC**: *Internal forces and moments*  
  - **Unit:** `LIT`  
  - **Default:** **YES**  
  - Meaning: enables printing section internal actions. Sub-modes exist under FORC:
    - **YES**: *total internal forces*
    - **FULL**: *single components*
    - **EXTR**: *single components with coordinates*

### 6) Load case selection
- **LC**: *Considered load cases*  
  - **Unit:** `LIT`  
  - **Default:** **YES**  
  - Meaning: includes a listing of the load cases processed.

### 7) Plot/graphical output switches
- **PLOT**: *All graphic options*  
  - **Unit:** `LIT`  
  - **Default:** `*` (implies “depends on other settings / not a fixed literal default”)
- Component-specific plot toggles (each default **YES**) are:
  - **NX**: normal force diagram
  - **VY**: shear force diagram
  - **VZ**: shear force diagram
  - **MX**: torsional moment diagram
  - **MY**: bending moment diagram (about y)
  - **MZ**: bending moment diagram (about z)
  - **V**: resultant shear force diagram
  - **M**: resultant moment diagram
  - **W**: warping parts diagram

These plot toggles correspond to the ability to selectively switch on/off individual graphical components.

---

## Rows under **Item = VAL**
This part defines whether an output option is suppressed or produced.  
- **VAL**: *Value of output option*  
  - **Unit:** `LIT`  
  - **Default:** `-`

Sub-options shown:
- **NO**: *No output*  
  - **Unit:** `LIT`  
  - **Default:** (not shown in the excerpt, but clearly indicates suppression behavior)

---

## Relationship to the described SIR behavior (from surrounding text)
The context indicates that SIR can produce **two tables per section** per run:
1) **Optional geometry table** (enabled by **GEO**)
2) **Summed resultant section components per load case** (primarily tied to **FORC** selections and load case handling)

It also notes:
- The database stores the **section definition and forces**; later interpretations overwrite/delete prior SIR data.
- Graphical representations can be produced for **every load case and every section component**, consistent with the plot keywords in the table.

In summary, the table functions as a **keyword-driven control sheet** defining whether SIR outputs geometry, internal forces, reinforcement, load case listings, support reactions, and which force/moment diagrams to plot.

ECHO
 YES
 —
 Regular output
 FULL Extensive output
 The output of SIR consists of two tables for each section. The first table is optional and de- scribes the geometry of the section and of all intersected elements.
 The second table lists the sum of all resultant section components for each load case. The user gets also the parts of all individual elements with ECHO FORC.
 A graphical representation may be produced for every load case and every section component.
 The individual components may be switched on or off with PLOT or the suboptions NX to W.
 The section definition and the forces for each load are saved in the data base for a later inter- pretation. In this case all already existing SIR-dates in the data base are overwritten and/or deleted.
 The type SUPPORTS with the sum of corresponding nodal forces and moments is printed additionally per load case in the list of the forces and moments considering ECHO REAC YES, FULL, EXTR or 4. All nodes inside the section box are used, independend of the group control. With ECHO REAC EXTR the resulting forces of bedding of the area elements are added. The used area elements are dependend from the group control. With ECHO REAC 4 the resulting forces of bedding of the area elements are used instead of the node support forces.
The content and the extent of the output are dependent on the definition of the record ECHO.

The list of the forces and moments is output with ECHO FORC YES. The overall internal forces and moments (type SUM) of the single load cases at the sections defined in the records SECT are printed.

content: The results of SIR can be stored in an input file for the programs AQUA and AQBS for the use of a classical beam design. The kind and the extent of these dates are described with the corresponding CTRL options.
The corresponding force and moment distributions are represented graphically in Report Browser output with the input ECHO PLOT YES or ECHO NX to W YES.
